prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of the gains from trade and of firm-level responses to trade costs

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework (Melitz 2003, with Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus foreign direct investment) moved trade analysis from representative industries to firms. It made selection, reallocation and the extensive margin central to who gains from trade, and it organised two decades of firm-level empirical work across many countries and datasets. The credit for the core model is unusually clean: one originating paper and one co-author who extended it in complementary directions. It is a distinct advance on the increasing-returns trade theory recognised in 2008, because it adds firm-level productivity differences and selection. It also speaks to the firm-level pricing, markup and market-power questions that industrial organisation and trade now share. After my reconsideration, this is the proposal where scientific importance, attribution clarity and maturity line up best for me. A two-person award also respects the cap of three unique laureates for the whole configuration.
statement.case_against: Credit for firm heterogeneity in trade is broader than the ballot names. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum documented the exporter facts and built closely related models, so a Melitz-Helpman award leaves out legitimate contributors. Quantitative welfare conclusions depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity and CES demand. Trade already has a prize (2008), so the Committee may see this as one field's turn coming round again. Helpman's wider body of trade work could also be recognised in a different framing.

responses.point: Boppart ranks the firm-heterogeneity work second and reads it as building on Krugman's 2008 prize without duplicating it. He flags that Redding may deserve a third slot and that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum contributed to the empirical foundation.
responses.response: I agree that it builds on rather than duplicates the 2008 prize, since selection on productivity is a new mechanism relative to love-of-variety and scale effects. On Redding I come out differently. His strongest contributions are the later quantitative and spatial extensions, which apply the framework rather than found it, so a third name would dilute a clean attribution. I take the Bernard-Jensen point more seriously. Their exporter-premium facts motivated the theory, so the citation should be framed around the theory of selection and the gains from trade, not around the empirical regularities, and the Committee should acknowledge that gap openly.

responses.point: Enflo ranks the heterogeneous-firm framework first as a field-transforming, durable contribution. She notes that Krugman's 2008 prize may reduce appetite for another trade award and that the exclusion of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is an obvious attribution issue.
responses.response: I share your view of its durability and of how widely firm-level trade data now use it. On field balance, I would not treat a past prize as a quota. Trade has had no recognition since 2008, and the question is whether this advance is separable and mature, which I think it is. I would qualify the attribution concern. Eaton-Kortum is a different, Ricardian strand, so it is less of a substitute for the Melitz mechanism than the Bernard-Jensen empirical work, which weakens the case for widening the group. I do accept that, given a two-person cap on this part, some of that empirical credit cannot be recognised.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the collateral-constraint credit-cycle work first. He sees Kiyotaki and Moore as the clean originators of a macro-finance mechanism that is mature, and he views its overlap with the 2022 prize as a modest concern.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution, and I ranked it second myself. The mechanism of collateral values feeding back into borrowing limits and asset prices is distinct from the bank-run and bank-intermediation results recognised in 2022. I do not make it my preferred part for a structural reason. A two-part configuration of Kiyotaki and Moore plus Melitz and Helpman would name four people, above the cap of three. Choosing between them, I weigh the broader empirical footprint of the firm-heterogeneity work. Part of the evidence for the credit-cycle channel is indirect, because calibrated models carry much of it, so I keep it as an alternative and not as my first choice.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee wants to credit Bernard, Eaton, Jensen or Kortum, or Redding, which would change the two-person attribution.
How much welfare conclusions on the gains from trade depend on Pareto and CES assumptions.
Whether the Committee treats trade as already covered by the 2008 prize.

I moved my opening first choice (B020, structural demand estimation) to an alternative. No colleague ranked it, its credit boundary spans seven names, and any trio of Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. I still think its scientific case is strong, and I would want colleagues' views on whether it is a methodological or an industrial-organisation award.
statement.conflict_note: My research is in industrial organisation and international trade, including exchange-rate pass-through, pricing under imperfect competition and firm-level data. That is close to B044 and B020, and I apply the same criteria as in other fields. I co-authored a 2026 IJIO paper with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen. It is not related to any shortlisted candidate. My spouse's public political role has no apparent bearing. I see no documented personal, institutional or co-authorship connection to the credited candidates, so no recusal appears required from the supplied profile.
